title: Zero Registered Slaughterhouses: Vietnam's Dog Meat Trade Has No Safety Net
excerpt: Vietnam's dog meat trade operates outside every food safety framework — and the data on public health consequences is impossible to ignore.
body_html:
Every year, an estimated 5 million dogs are killed for meat in Vietnam. Not one of those animals passes through a registered slaughterhouse. Not one transaction falls under a licensed food safety inspection regime. This is not a loophole — it is a total absence of regulatory infrastructure, and it carries measurable consequences for the people who live alongside this trade every day.

Vietnam's food safety law requires all meat intended for human consumption to be processed in licensed, inspected facilities. Dog meat is consumed widely, yet exists entirely outside this framework. The supply chain — from capture to slaughter to sale — is unregulated at every stage. This means no veterinary checks, no temperature controls, no pathogen screening, and no traceability. The result is documented: the dog meat trade is a recognised vector for rabies transmission, as well as contamination by E. coli and Salmonella. These are not theoretical risks. They are recorded public health outcomes occurring in communities across the country.

The international evidence on what follows a ban is instructive. South Korea, which legislated against dog meat slaughter in 2024, cited public health improvement as a primary driver alongside shifting public attitudes. The Philippines enacted its ban in 1998 and recorded measurable reductions in rabies-linked incidents in affected provinces over the following decade. In both cases, enforcement became possible precisely because a clear legal line existed. You cannot enforce a standard that has never been set.

The conversation in Vietnam is already happening — and it is being led by Vietnamese people. A 2021 survey found that 95% of respondents in Vietnam support ending the dog and cat meat trade. Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City have both issued formal guidance encouraging residents to stop consuming dog meat, citing public health and reputational concerns. The public will exists. The regulatory framework to match it does not — yet. What Vietnam's food safety authorities have the power to do is create the legal architecture that reflects what the population already believes.

Regulation is not the enemy of culture or livelihoods. It is the mechanism by which a society protects its people. A trade that cannot meet any standard of food safety inspection is, by definition, a trade that cannot be made safe. The path forward is the one that 95% of the Vietnamese public already supports: ending the dog meat trade, and replacing an unregulated vacuum with enforceable law. Lucky, a nine-year-old Ta dog and family companion, represents the millions of animals and the thousands of families that stand to benefit from exactly that change.
